en: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Wild Wood Beach, Cape May County, New Jersey, 1890, Sheet 24

sheet-24.description: The oceanfront core of Wild Wood Beach, the resort that became the city of Wildwood, drawn in 1890 at 60 feet to an inch with north toward the upper right and the Atlantic Ocean at the foot of the sheet. Five avenues run down the sheet toward the beach, Cedar, Oak, Wild Wood, Pine and Maple Avenues, and are crossed by Pacific Avenue, Atlantic Avenue and Ocean Avenue, which runs along the beach with no blocks on its seaward side. Twelve numbered blocks are laid out in full with their lot lines and lot numbers, but very few are built on. The buildings are mostly scattered frame dwellings, with a store and office on Oak Avenue near Atlantic Avenue and two larger buildings: the Sea View House at Pacific and Cedar Avenues, a three-storey boarding house, and the Hotel Dayton on Atlantic Avenue between Oak and Wild Wood Avenues. On the beach at the foot of Oak Avenue stand a pavilion, a row of bath houses and a photograph gallery. A note at the top of the Cedar to Oak block gives the distance to the railroad, 125 feet beyond the sheet. Outlines of blocks west of Cedar Avenue are drawn without lots, with one dwelling. The sheet carries a large compass rose and a scale bar of 60 feet to one inch.
notes: Cedar, Oak, Wild Wood, Pine and Maple Avenues are today East Cedar, East Oak, East Wildwood, East Pine and East Maple Avenues; Pacific and Atlantic Avenues keep their names.
Ocean Avenue was the beachfront street in 1890; modern Ocean Avenue lies about 25 m further toward the sea and was not used as control.
Sea View House, Hotel Dayton and the beach pavilion are the named buildings.
The north arrow was not used; the fitted rotation is about 47 degrees.

Wild Wood Beach (now Wildwood, between East Cedar and East Maple Avenues, Pacific Avenue to the beach), printed sheet 24 of the Cape May series, 1890, 60 ft to an inch, north to the upper right (fitted rotation about 47 deg; the drawn north arrow is not used). One part: Cedar, Oak, Wild Wood, Pine and Maple Avs crossed by Pacific, Atlantic and Ocean Avs. Ocean Av (the beachfront) is left out: modern Ocean Avenue lies about 25 m further seaward.
